nameStory: The black-sided pygmy grasshopper gets its name from the distinctive dark stripes that run along its sides, contrasting with its lighter body. The word 'pygmy' refers to its tiny size compared to the familiar meadow grasshoppers we usually see hopping through summer grass. It's also called a 'grouse locust' because early naturalists thought its mottled, earth-toned coloring resembled the camouflaged plumage of grouse birds.
description: The black-sided pygmy grasshopper is a tiny, ground-dwelling insect that's easy to overlook despite being fairly common. These miniature grasshoppers are much smaller than their familiar green cousins, typically less than half an inch long. They have a distinctive shield-like plate (called a pronotum) that extends back over most of their body like a little roof. Their mottled brown and gray coloring helps them blend perfectly with soil, leaf litter, and muddy ground.

idTips.label: Dark side stripes
idTips.description: Look for prominent black or very dark brown stripes running along each side of the body - these are the 'black sides' that give this species its name

idTips.label: Shield-like back plate
idTips.description: The pronotum (back plate) extends like a pointed roof over most of the abdomen, feeling firm and slightly ridged if you gently touch it

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: About the size of your pinky fingernail or smaller - much tinier than common grass grasshoppers

idTips.label: Mottled earth tones
idTips.description: Overall coloring is a mix of browns, grays, and sometimes hints of olive, creating a speckled appearance that matches dirt and dead leaves

idTips.label: Ground-hugging behavior
idTips.description: Stays very close to the ground and moves with short, quick hops rather than the long leaps of larger grasshoppers

habitat: Look for black-sided pygmy grasshoppers in moist areas with bare or sparsely vegetated soil, especially along pond edges, stream banks, and wet meadows. They favor muddy spots where the ground stays damp, often hiding among sedges, rushes, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll also find them in marshy areas and the muddy margins of temporary pools after spring rains.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and are most active, often seen hopping along muddy ground as snow melts and reveals bare soil. Look for them on warm, sunny days near water sources.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity continues through early summer, with mating and egg-laying occurring. They remain close to moist ground even during dry periods.
seasonality.fall: Activity begins to slow as temperatures drop, though some adults may persist into early fall. They become less active and harder to spot.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off and the species overwinters as eggs in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to hatch into tiny nymphs.

funFact: These tiny grasshoppers are amazing swimmers and can actually dive underwater to escape predators, using their powerful hind legs to 'fly' through the water just like they hop on land!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other pygmy grasshoppers, but the black side stripes are your best clue - think 'racing stripes' along a tiny brown race car. Other pygmy grasshoppers in the area usually lack these distinct dark lateral markings.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'grasshoppers,' pygmy grasshoppers belong to a different family (Tetrigidae) than common grasshoppers and have quite different lifestyles. They're more closely related to crickets than to meadow grasshoppers, and they prefer algae and decaying plant matter over fresh grass.
compareHints: The black-sided pygmy grasshopper can be distinguished from its close relative, the pointed-tail pygmy grasshopper (Tettigidea acuta), by its prominent dark side stripes and slightly more robust build. While both species have the characteristic shield-like back plate, the black-sided version has more contrasting coloration and tends to prefer muddier, wetter habitats than its cousin.
